title: Plan on the pull request, apply on merge
summary: The pipeline every Terraform team ends up with: fmt, validate and tflint first, a saved plan posted for review, the same plan applied after merge with the environment's own identity. Then make a failing repo's CI pass.

steps.title: The pipeline
body: permissions: { id-token: write, contents: read, pull-requests: write }
concurrency: terraform-prod                 # never two runs against prod's state at once
- uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v6   # OIDC: no stored keys
- run: terraform show -no-color tfplan > plan.txt    # posted as a PR comment
environment: production                 # a required reviewer approves here
# ...same setup, an apply role, download the artifact, then:
Key decisions: **read-only credentials for plan, write credentials only for apply** (the plan role cannot change
anything, so a malicious pull request cannot either); **the merged plan is the one applied** (a stale plan fails
safely); **one run at a time per state**. Tools such as Atlantis, HCP Terraform, Spacelift or env0 package the same
flow with plan comments and approvals built in.

steps.prompt: Put a pull request's CI steps in order (cheapest checks first).
lines: terraform show -no-color tfplan  # post it on the PR
also: terraform show -no-color tfplan  # post it on the PR
steps.explain: `fmt` needs nothing; `validate` needs `init` (providers for the schema) but no credentials; `tflint` and `validate` can swap; `plan` is the expensive step that talks to the cloud. Failing fast saves minutes on every push.

steps.title: fmt, validate, tflint: what each one catches
body: | `terraform fmt -check -recursive` | layout differences (exit 3); `-diff` shows them | nothing |
| `terraform validate` | syntax, unknown arguments, wrong types, references to things that do not exist | `init` (use `-backend=false` in CI lint jobs) |

| `tflint` | valid code that is still wrong or sloppy: unused declarations, untyped variables, missing version constraints, deprecated syntax; with provider rulesets, an `instance_type` that does not exist | a `.tflint.hcl` |
`terraform validate` checks the **configuration**; it never knows whether an AMI exists or a name is taken. tflint's
`recommended` preset (the bundled `terraform` ruleset) is a good default; provider rulesets (`tflint-ruleset-aws`,
`-azurerm`, `-google`) add cloud knowledge. Run all three locally with one command (`make ci`, a pre-commit hook) so
CI is never the first to tell you.

steps.title: Make CI green
prompt: `~/infra/shop-repo` is a pull request whose CI is red. CI runs `make ci` (`cat Makefile`): fmt, validate, tflint.
Run `make ci` and fix each failure **properly**, in the order they appear: format the files, fix what `validate`
reports, and fix what `tflint` reports (do not silence rules: no `tflint-ignore`, no changes to `.tflint.hcl` or the
`Makefile`). The `retention_days` input must stay and must actually be used: put it in the rendered JSON as

checks.name: make ci passes
checks.fail: `make ci` still fails (the end of its output is shown).

checks.name: nothing silenced
checks.cmd: cd ~/infra/shop-repo && ! grep -rq 'tflint-ignore' --include='*.tf' . && git diff --quiet HEAD -- .tflint.hcl Makefile && test "$(git log --format=%H -- .tflint.hcl Makefile | wc -l)" = 1
checks.fail: Fix the code, not the rules: no `tflint-ignore` comments, and `.tflint.hcl` and `Makefile` unchanged.

checks.name: retention_days is typed and used
checks.cmd: cd ~/infra/shop-repo/envs/prod && rm -rf /tmp/ci && cp -r ../.. /tmp/ci && cd /tmp/ci/envs/prod && terraform init -input=false -no-color >/dev/null && terraform apply -auto-approve -input=false -no-color >/dev/null && jq -e '.retention_days == 30 and .env == "prod"' out/prod/notify.json >/dev/null

checks.name: committed
checks.cmd: cd ~/infra/shop-repo && test -z "$(git status --porcelain)" && test "$(git rev-list --count HEAD)" -ge 2
checks.fail: Commit your fixes: `git status` should be clean.

hints: `terraform fmt -recursive` fixes the layout. `make validate` then reports *Unsupported attribute* on `module.notify.filenme`: the module's output is called `file`.
tflint reports `retention_days` has no type and is declared but unused. Give it `type = number` and use it in the `jsonencode({...})`.

`sed -i 's/module.notify.filenme/module.notify.file/' envs/prod/main.tf`, add `type = number` to the variable, add `retention_days = var.retention_days` to the JSON, `terraform fmt -recursive`, `make ci`, commit.
solution: sed -i 's/^  description = "How long alert history is kept."$/  type        = number\n  description = "How long alert history is kept."/' modules/notify/main.tf
sed -i 's/^    channels = var.channels$/    channels       = var.channels\n    retention_days = var.retention_days/' modules/notify/main.tf
git commit -m "Fix formatting, the output reference, and type and use retention_days"
steps.explain: Each tool caught a different class of mistake: layout (fmt), a broken reference (validate), and an input that was accepted and then silently ignored (tflint). That last one is the dangerous kind: the caller set `retention_days = 30` and believed it worked.

steps.prompt: Why does the plan job use a role that can only **read** the cloud account, while only the apply job (after merge and approval) can write?
options: Plans run code from unreviewed pull requests; with a read-only role, a malicious or broken PR still cannot change anything (an `external` data source or a provider could run arbitrary code)
Terraform refuses to plan with write permissions
steps.explain: `terraform plan` executes providers and can run programs (`data "external"`), so it is code execution with the job's credentials. Separate identities per stage and per environment, short-lived through OIDC, are the standard answer.
